summary: Sāmaṇera Bodhesako (1939–1988) was a Buddhist studies scholar. He founded Path Press and served as an editor at the Buddhist Publication Society.
Sīlaratano studied under Narada Maha Thera, Nyanaponika Thera, and Ajahn Maha Bua (~1977–2011).

Sōen Shaku (1860–1919) worked in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and religious studies. He studied at Keio University and under teachers including Kosen Imakita, whom he succeeded. He served as Zen master at Engaku-ji (1892) and president of Hanazono University (1914–1917).
Sōkatsu Shaku (1870–1954) was a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies. He studied under Kosen Imakita (1889) and Sōen Shaku (1893), and founded Ryōbōkai (1901, 1906) and Ningen Zen Kyodan.

Sōkō Morinaga (1925–1995) was a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar. He studied at Toyama High School and Daitoku-ji under Sesso Oda and Zuigan Goto. He served as head of Hanazono University (1986–1994) and head priest at Daiju-in (~1963–1995).

T. Chandrasekharan worked in Indology and studied under S. Kuppuswami Sastri. Succeeding T. R. Chintamani, he served as Professor of History of Sanskrit Language and Literature at Madras Sanskrit College (attested 1951).

T. Griffith Foulk, specializing in Buddhist studies, Japanology, and Sinology, earned his PhD at the University of Michigan (~1978–1987) under Luis O. Gómez. He taught at Michigan (~1987–1995) and Sarah Lawrence College, where he became Riggs Professor of Religion (attested 2015).
T. K. V. Desikachar (1938–2016) worked in Indology and religious studies. He studied under Tirumalai Krishnamacharya (~1961–1989) and founded the Krishnamacharya Yoga Mandiram in 1976.

T. N. Ramachandran (1901–1973) specialized in Indology and archaeology. He served as an archaeologist at the Government Museum, Chennai (~1928–1934) and as curator of archaeology at the National Museum, New Delhi.
T. R. Chintamani was an Indologist who studied under S. Kuppuswami Sastri. He served as Senior Lecturer in Sanskrit at the University of Madras (attested 1938–1951).

T. R. V. Murti (1902–1986) worked in Indology, philosophy, and Buddhist studies. He earned a D.Litt. at Banaras Hindu University under Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, later holding professorships at BHU (~1953–1967) and McMaster University (attested 1982), and a post at Oxford (~1959–1960).
T. S. Srinivasa Sastri worked in Indology and philosophy. He held posts at the Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute (attested 1972), where he served as Professor (attested 1984–1992).

T. V. Ramachandra Dikshitar was an Indology and philosophy scholar. He served as Principal of Madras Sanskrit College (attested 1938) and as Professor of Advaita Vedānta at Banaras Hindu University (attested 1946).

T. V. Venkatachala Sastry (born 1933) is a linguist and Indologist. He studied at the University of Mysore, where his supervisors included D. L. Narasimhachar and Harogadde Manappa Nayak, and served there as lecturer (1968) and Professor (1984–1994).

T. Venkatacharya was an Indology and linguistics scholar. He held a post at the Italian Institute for the Middle and Far East and served as Professor in the Department of East Asian Studies at the University of Toronto (attested 1971).

T. W. Rhys Davids (1843–1922) was an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar who earned his PhD at the University of Breslau under Adolf Friedrich Stenzler. He founded the Pali Text Society, held chairs at London and Manchester, and co-founded the British Academy.
T. Y. Lee is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Mangala Vihara and the Buddhist and Pali College of Singapore.

Tadao Yoshikawa (born 1937) is a scholar of Sinology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies who studied at Kyoto University. He held posts at Kyoto University (1974, 1984–2000), Ryukoku University (2002), Hanazono University (~2000–2008), and Toho Gakkai (~2009–2011).

Tadashi Inoue (1929–2014) worked in archaeology and Buddhist studies, studying at the University of Tokyo. His career included roles at Kyoto National Museum, director of Iida City Museum (1988–2006), and professorships at Nara, Bukkyo, and Kyoto Arts universities.
Tadashi Sekino (1868–1935) was a scholar of archaeology, Sinology, and Buddhist studies. He studied at the University of Tokyo (~1892–1895) and later served there as professor emeritus (~1929–1935).
